CORRECTED SUBMISSION PACKAGE

This package was rebuilt from the 31 PDFs in T01-DocsSet.zip. Full text was extracted from every page for corpus-level analysis. Bibliographic fields were cross-checked against PDF metadata and first-page title blocks where possible. The five Word reports correspond to Tasks 1–5. Document_Inventory.csv contains the full inventory including keywords, themes and automated relevant excerpts.

Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan
Automated corpus inventory, metadata extraction and first-pass evidence scan
Evidence base: 31 PDFs from T01-DocsSet.zip
1. Method
The ZIP was unpacked into 31 PDF documents. Text was extracted from every page of every PDF. Bibliographic metadata were taken from embedded PDF metadata when reliable and cross-checked against the first page; missing or truncated fields were reconstructed from the visible title block. Keywords, thematic tags and short relevant passages were then extracted automatically from the first pages and full-text signals. This corrected version avoids treating arbitrary abstract text as author metadata.
2. Corpus at a glance
The corpus is strongly concentrated around production scheduling and energy efficiency, with a second layer devoted to uncertainty/robustness and a newer layer covering deep reinforcement learning, Digital Twins, explainability and human-centric decision support. The documents span classical operations research, metaheuristics, data-driven control and Industry 5.0 perspectives.
3. Document inventory
4. Initial observations
Energy is not treated as a stand-alone engineering variable: many papers formulate a joint scheduling problem balancing energy, tardiness, throughput, stability or production penalties.
Uncertainty is a recurring reason to move beyond deterministic schedules: breakdowns, processing-time variation, release-time uncertainty, energy supply/demand uncertainty and electricity-price uncertainty all appear in the corpus.
DRL is positioned mainly as an online/adaptive decision mechanism, while mathematical programming and metaheuristics remain important for constraints, benchmarks, offline optimization and smaller or structured instances.
Digital Twins provide the virtual/physical synchronization layer needed for live monitoring, simulation and what-if evaluation.
XAI and human-centric papers highlight a deployment gap: a high-performing scheduler is not automatically acceptable if planners cannot understand, contest or safely override its decisions.
The accompanying Document_Inventory.csv contains the complete fields requested in the task, including keywords and the automatically captured relevant excerpt for each document.

2. Topic concentration
The densest area of the corpus is the intersection of scheduling, energy and optimization. This is useful strategically because it means the evidence base is strongest for improving operational efficiency rather than for replacing the entire production-control stack with a single AI technique.
3. Relationship network
The network shows that uncertainty/robustness and real-time control act as bridges between conventional scheduling and learning-based approaches. Digital Twin papers connect the optimization layer to plant data and simulation, while XAI/human-centric papers connect algorithmic performance to adoption and governance.
4. Dense zones and white spaces
Dense zone: energy-efficient scheduling of furnaces, heat treatment and steel operations using mathematical optimization or metaheuristics.
Dense zone: robustness under operational uncertainty, especially when schedules must survive disturbances rather than only optimize a nominal plan.
Emerging zone: DRL for dynamic energy-aware scheduling and demand response.
Integration zone: Digital Twins as the operational bridge between data, simulation and scheduling.
White space: relatively few papers integrate steel-specific DRL + Digital Twin + XAI + explicit human override in one validated industrial architecture. This gap becomes the opportunity explored in Tasks 3–4.

Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence
Contradictions, trade-offs and decision-relevant tensions
Evidence base: 31 PDFs from T01-DocsSet.zip
1. Divergence 1 — Optimality vs responsiveness
Classical optimization offers explicit objectives, constraints and, in some formulations, optimality guarantees. The furnace and steel scheduling papers based on MILP, robust optimization, decomposition and polynomial-time algorithms demonstrate why these methods remain valuable. Their limitation appears when the environment changes faster than a full optimization model can be rebuilt or solved. Dynamic rescheduling and DRL papers address this by prioritizing rapid online decisions.
Management implication: do not frame the choice as “optimization or AI.” Use exact/robust models where structure and guarantees matter, and adaptive policies where disturbances and online latency dominate.
2. Divergence 2 — Energy efficiency vs production service level
The corpus repeatedly treats energy as one objective among several. Heat-treatment, reheating-furnace and hot-strip-mill studies balance energy with tardiness, makespan, rolling penalties or schedule stability. A schedule that minimizes energy alone can shift work, increase waiting or degrade delivery performance. Conversely, a throughput-only policy can ignore expensive peaks and idle-energy losses.
Management implication: the scheduler needs a multi-objective policy with explicit business weights or Pareto choices, not a single energy KPI.
3. Divergence 3 — Nominal efficiency vs robustness
Deterministic schedules can be efficient under expected conditions but fragile under breakdowns, uncertain release times, processing-time variation and volatile energy conditions. Proactive and robust scheduling papers deliberately sacrifice some nominal efficiency to preserve stability. DRL papers attempt to learn adaptive responses, but their robustness depends on the quality and breadth of training scenarios.
Management implication: evaluate solutions under stress scenarios and distribution shifts, not only on average-case test data.
4. Divergence 4 — Performance vs explainability
The XAI papers show a second deployment tension. Genetic algorithms and DRL can produce effective decisions while remaining opaque to planners. Counterfactual explanations, adapted XAI techniques and explainable DRL attempt to translate model behavior into reasons and actionable alternatives. However, explanations themselves add design complexity and must be tailored to the operator’s decision context.
Management implication: explanation quality should be treated as a system requirement—alongside cost, energy and latency—rather than as a visualization added after model development.
5. Divergence 5 — Automation vs human authority
Human-centric and process-safety papers caution against assuming that autonomy is always the objective. In high-consequence process environments, human expertise, situational awareness and override capability remain important. Digital Twins can improve this relationship by allowing operators to inspect predicted consequences before execution.
Management implication: target intelligence augmentation first: AI proposes and continuously optimizes; humans supervise exceptions, policy boundaries and safety-critical changes.

Task 4 — Integrative Synthesis
A deployable architecture combining optimization, DRL, Digital Twins and XAI
Evidence base: 31 PDFs from T01-DocsSet.zip
1. Integrated proposal
The evidence supports a hybrid architecture rather than a single “winning” algorithm. The proposed system uses the Digital Twin as the shared operational model, conventional optimization as the constraint/benchmark layer, DRL as the fast adaptive decision layer, and XAI plus human supervision as the trust and governance layer.
2. Architecture
1. Physical steel process & IoT
Collect furnace temperatures, equipment state, job progress, ladle/rolling status, energy prices and energy-system variables.
2. Digital Twin
Maintain a synchronized virtual representation; estimate hidden state; run what-if scenarios; generate safe training and validation scenarios.
3. Constraint & optimization layer
Encode metallurgical, sequencing, capacity, quality and safety constraints. MILP/robust/metaheuristic solvers produce baselines and feasible envelopes.
4. DRL decision layer
Choose rapid scheduling/rescheduling actions inside the feasible envelope, conditioned on current and recent observations. Reward combines energy cost, tardiness, throughput, stability and constraint penalties.
5. XAI layer
Provide feature/decision rationales, counterfactuals (“what would change this recommendation?”), expected KPI impact and confidence/novelty warnings.
6. Human supervisory layer
Planner approves policy changes and high-impact exceptions, can override actions, and feeds outcomes back into the system.
7. Continuous assurance
Compare AI decisions against optimization baselines, detect drift, retrain offline in the Twin, and promote new policies only after safety/performance gates.
3. Operating principles
Hard constraints remain outside the learned reward whenever possible; the AI should not “learn” whether a metallurgical or safety constraint may be violated.
Train offline first using historical and synthetic disturbance scenarios generated through the Digital Twin; use shadow mode before closed-loop execution.
Use a multi-objective reward with business-owned weights and explicit reporting of trade-offs.
Escalate unfamiliar states, low-confidence recommendations and safety-relevant deviations to a human planner.
Keep a deterministic fallback schedule/controller so production does not depend on the availability of the AI stack.
4. Phased implementation roadmap
5. KPIs
Primary KPIs: energy cost per tonne, total energy consumption, tardiness/service level, throughput, schedule stability/rescheduling frequency and peak demand. Assurance KPIs: hard-constraint violations, human override rate, explanation usefulness, policy drift, decision latency and fallback activations.
Phase | Scope | Deliverable | Gate
0 — Data readiness | One furnace/line | Clean event model + KPI baseline | Data completeness and clock alignment
1 — Digital Twin | Selected process | Validated simulation / state estimator | Twin reproduces key operational KPIs
2 — Decision support | Offline/shadow | Optimization + DRL recommendations | No constraint violations; measurable KPI uplift
3 — Human-supervised pilot | Limited live scope | XAI dashboard + approval workflow | Planner acceptance and stable performance
4 — Controlled automation | Low-risk decisions | Automatic actions within safe envelope | Drift, rollback and audit controls proven
5 — Scale | Adjacent furnaces/lines | Reusable architecture | Benefits persist across contexts

Task 5 — Final Report & Strategic Storytelling
Executive synthesis using AIDA: Attention → Interest → Desire → Action
Evidence base: 31 PDFs from T01-DocsSet.zip
Executive message
Steel scheduling is simultaneously an operations, energy and uncertainty problem. The 31-document evidence base shows that no single method resolves all three dimensions. The strongest strategic direction is a staged hybrid system that combines rigorous optimization, adaptive DRL, a Digital Twin and explainable human supervision.
A — Attention: energy and operational complexity are coupled
Furnaces, rolling, steelmaking and material-handling decisions determine not only throughput but also idle energy, reheating demand, electricity exposure and downstream stability. The literature shows that scheduling itself is an energy-management lever. At the same time, breakdowns, uncertain release/processing times and volatile energy conditions make a static optimum short-lived.
I — Interest: the technology pieces already exist
The corpus contains mature optimization approaches for furnace and steel scheduling, robust formulations for uncertainty, metaheuristics for large multi-objective problems, DRL for fast energy-aware decisions, and Digital Twin architectures for live state synchronization and simulation. XAI and counterfactual methods add the missing ability to explain recommendations to planners.
D — Desire: combine strengths instead of replacing proven control
A hybrid architecture reduces adoption risk. The Digital Twin supplies context and a safe experimentation environment. Optimization defines feasible, auditable baselines. DRL reacts quickly inside those boundaries. XAI explains the recommendation and its alternatives. Human supervision protects against unfamiliar or high-consequence situations. This preserves industrial discipline while adding adaptive intelligence.
A — Action: start with one bounded pilot
Select one energy-intensive scheduling scope—such as a reheating furnace or a tightly defined steelmaking scheduling segment—with reliable data and measurable pain points. Build the Twin and baseline first, run DRL in shadow mode, expose explanations to planners, and only automate low-risk decisions after predefined gates are met. Scale only after benefits survive disturbance tests and real operating conditions.
Recommended 90-day management agenda
Weeks 1–3: define process boundary, owners, hard constraints, baseline KPIs and data quality requirements.
Weeks 4–6: construct and validate the Digital Twin; reproduce current scheduling behavior and key energy/throughput KPIs.
Weeks 7–9: benchmark MILP/robust/metaheuristic approaches and train a DRL policy on historical + synthetic disturbances.
Weeks 10–11: deploy shadow-mode recommendations with XAI/counterfactual explanations and collect planner feedback.
Week 12: gate review. Proceed to a supervised live pilot only if performance, robustness, explanation quality and safety criteria are all satisfied.
Final recommendation
Treat AI-enabled scheduling as a controlled capability build, not a one-step automation project. The corpus supports a progression from data and Digital Twin readiness, through benchmark optimization and shadow-mode DRL, to explainable human-supervised automation. This directly addresses the business objectives of reducing operational complexity, improving energy efficiency and introducing intelligent automation without discarding proven industrial constraints and expertise.
Evidence clusters used
The synthesis draws on all 31 supplied PDFs. Particularly central clusters are: furnace/green scheduling and idle-energy optimization; robust steel rolling and steelmaking scheduling under uncertainty; energy-aware steel scheduling and demand response using DRL; Digital Twin applications in reheating furnaces, rolling and live production planning; and XAI/human-centric work on explainable scheduling, counterfactuals, production control and process safety.
